# Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models

Hyunwoo Ryu ^(†)^(†)thanks: Equal contribution.    Eric M. Chen^(\*)   
Max Wilcoxson^(\*)    Vincent Sitzmann Affiliation: Computer Science &
Artificial Intelligence Laboratory Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute
of Technology Affiliation: Cambridge, MA 02139, USA
Email: [{hwryu,echen01,mwil,sitzmann}@mit.edu](mailto:)

###### Abstract

Video generative models are an emerging tool for embodied agents: they
can serve as scalable visual planners, generating videos that depict how
to complete previously unseen tasks. However, executing these plans
typically requires a video-to-action or “inverse dynamics” model trained
on large, human-collected video-action datasets, severely limiting
scalability. We introduce Mirror, a self-supervised approach that learns
video-to-action mappings through environment interactions, without prior
action data or hand-crafted rewards. Mirror learns by attempting to
follow a visual plan by executing its best guess of the underlying
actions in the environment. Mirror then trains on the resulting
video-action pairs, incrementally self-improving and following the
visual planner more closely. Across Atari, OGBench, and DeepMind
Control, Mirror outperforms leading learning-from-observation methods
with learned video plans, and achieves near-expert performance with
oracle plans. On Minecraft BASALT, it outperforms methods with access to
expert actions or hand-engineered task knowledge. In Minecraft survival,
it is the first method to acquire an iron pickaxe through
self-improvement alone, without rewards or expert action labels. In the
offline setting, with expert action labels but no environment
interaction, it sets a new state of the art in obtaining diamonds. Our
results suggest that advances in video models can translate into
increasingly capable agents without a corresponding need for
hand-crafted rewards or large collections of expert action data. Please
find video and other results on our
[website.](https://wilcoxsonm21.github.io/mirror/)

|     |
| --- |
|     |

## 1 Introduction

Video models are emerging as scalable learners of the physical world.
Trained on vast collections of unstructured web video, they absorb
knowledge about objects, environments, human behavior, and how tasks
unfold over time. Recent work has begun to harness this knowledge for
robot control by using video models as _visual planners_ (e.g.,  [Du
et al., 2023](#bib.bib11); [Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib8); [Ye et al.,
2026](#bib.bib67); [Rhoda, 2026](#bib.bib48)). Given past frames and
optional task conditioning, these models generate a video depicting how
the task could be completed. An embodiment-specific video-to-action
(V2A) or “inverse dynamics” model then translates the generated visual
trajectory into robot actions. This has yielded impressive
generalization across unseen tasks, objects, environments, and
embodiments.

However, training the V2A model still requires significant amounts of
expert-collected, paired video-action data from oracle motion planners
or human teleoperation. Moreover, agents cannot easily generate such
video-action data by rolling out random policies in the environment, as
critical environment transitions—such as executing a robot grasp or
crafting a diamond pickaxe in Minecraft—are unreachable by a random
policy. Today, video planners thus inherit the same scalability
bottleneck as video-language-action models: a reliance on expensive
expert teleoperation data.

In this paper, we introduce Mirror, a _fully self-supervised_ method for
learning to execute the policy encoded by a video model only by
interacting with the world, without any expert video-action data. We
assume access to an expert video planner that, given the current agent
observation, can generate an expert-level visual plan. Under this
assumption, we show that no further expert action supervision or
hand-crafted rewards are necessary to achieve expert-level performance.
Mirror thus represents a bet on the continued scaling of video models:
as visual planners improve, their capabilities can be translated into
actions without a corresponding increase in expert action data.

Our key idea is to let a randomly initialized video-to-action model
self-improve against the expert video planner. Given the current agent
state, we query the planner to generate a video plan. The current
video-to-action model then predicts the corresponding actions and the
agent executes them in the environment. Interactions produce new paired
video-action data, which is used to improve the video-to-action model.
Critically, this data is not random but concentrated at the frontier of
the agent’s current capability to follow the video plan. Repeating this
process allows the agent to follow progressively more of the plan until
it faithfully reproduces the planner’s behavior. Mirror does not require
rewards, privileged state information, verifiers, or trajectory
filtering. Furthermore, we show that our self-improving approach can
outperform training on expert actions.

We evaluate Mirror in two settings: (i) the Minecraft survival
challenge ([Guss et al., 2019](#bib.bib17)) and Minecraft BASALT
competition tasks ([Shah et al., 2021](#bib.bib52)); and (ii) standard
decision-making benchmarks, including Atari ([Bellemare et al.,
2013](#bib.bib4)), OGBench ([Park et al., 2025a](#bib.bib46)), and
DeepMind Control ([Tassa et al., 2018](#bib.bib54)). To the best of our
knowledge, no prior method without either hand-crafted rewards or expert
action labels achieves non-zero success on these Minecraft tasks. Mirror
outperforms baselines, including those with privileged information, and
further exploits the emergent in-context learning of large video models,
improving faster than a baseline that cannot leverage context across
attempts.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- •
  Mirror, a scalable agent that learns long-horizon tasks by
  self-improving against a pre-trained video planner, without task
  rewards or expert video-action data.
- •
  A heavily adapted 14B-parameter NVIDIA Cosmos3 video planner with
  efficient long-context planning via causal KV-caching. Code and
  weights will be available soon on
  our [website](https://wilcoxsonm21.github.io/mirror/).
- •
  Mirror is the first method to achieve non-zero success rates on the
  BASALT Minecraft suite without expert video-action data or hard-coded
  actions.
- •
  In Minecraft survival, Mirror is the first method to obtain an iron
  pickaxe through self-improvement alone, using neither rewards nor
  expert action labels. Trained offline with action labels, it sets a
  new state of the art, obtaining diamonds nearly eight times as often
  as Dreamer V4.
- •
  On a suite of 24 common RL tasks, Mirror outperforms baselines using a
  generative video planner, and, when paired with an oracle video
  planner, nearly matches expert returns.

## 2 Related Work

Video planners. A nascent line of work leverages video generative models
to generate a visual plan of how a given task should be solved, and then
translates it into actions ([Du et al., 2023](#bib.bib11); [Ko et al.,
2024](#bib.bib25); [Liang et al., 2024a](#bib.bib29); [Luo & Du,
2024](#bib.bib36); [Bharadhwaj et al., 2024](#bib.bib5)). As video
models can be pre-trained on web-scale data, robots can inherit
impressive generalization capabilities ([Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib8);
[Li et al., 2026](#bib.bib28)). However, translating videos into robot
actions generally requires training on paired video-action data ([Du
et al., 2023](#bib.bib11); [Tian et al., 2025](#bib.bib56); [Pai et al.,
2025](#bib.bib44)). Our agent learns to act from video and self-play in
an interactive environment alone, reaching imagined futures without a
single action label.

Learning from demonstrations. We focus on imitation from observation,
where an agent learns from expert observations without action labels or
task rewards ([Torabi et al., 2018](#bib.bib58)). Adversarial approaches
match expert observation distributions through learned discriminator
rewards ([Torabi et al., 2019](#bib.bib59); [Liu et al.,
2023](#bib.bib33); [Giammarino et al., 2024](#bib.bib16)), but can be
unstable and sensitive to hyperparameters ([Huang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib22)). Iterative behavioral cloning alternates between
training a V2A model on the agent’s own experience and imitating
V2A-labeled demonstrations ([Torabi et al., 2018](#bib.bib58)), but
collecting informative transitions remains an exploration challenge on
long-horizon tasks ([Schmidt & Jiang, 2024](#bib.bib50)).
ASH ([Schneider et al., 2026](#bib.bib51)) applied a similar recipe to
long-horizon games such as Pokémon and Zelda, training an inverse
dynamics model on the agent’s own trajectories to pseudo-label internet
gameplay videos. Latent-action approaches such as LAPO and LAPA still
ground their latent actions with action labels or rewards ([Schmidt &
Jiang, 2024](#bib.bib50); [Ye et al., 2025](#bib.bib66)). Mirror instead
uses a video planner to guide exploration, collecting V2A training data
without action labels, rewards, or adversarial optimization.

Minecraft agents. Minecraft has become a standard benchmark for
long-horizon decision making, ranging from the fuzzy objectives of
BASALT ([Shah et al., 2021](#bib.bib52)) to the canonical MineRL
challenges ([Guss et al., 2019](#bib.bib17)). Existing agents rely on
some combination of expert action demonstrations and hand-designed
rewards. For example, VPT ([Baker et al., 2022](#bib.bib3)) trains a
behavioral cloning (BC) policy using about 2,000 hours of action-labeled
gameplay recordings from paid contractors, then fine-tunes the policy
with about 230,000 hours of online RL. While Dreamer V3 ([Hafner et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib18)) trains a Minecraft RL agent with only 1,400 hours of
online RL, they simplify parts of the Minecraft action space and still
require hand-designed reward. Dreamer V4 ([Hafner et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib19)) likewise uses reward, and also requires expert
actions to train a video world model. Pan-4B ([Pantograph,
2026](#bib.bib45)) trains a goal-conditioned RL policy on 500k hours of
internet video, yet still post-trains on 2,000 hours of expert action
labels. To make long-horizon tasks more tractable, many works improve
upon Minecraft policies with language models. MineDojo ([Fan et al.,
2022](#bib.bib14)) trains PPO agents on shaped rewards and a learned
video-language critic, while STEVE-1 ([Lifshitz et al.,
2023](#bib.bib31)), DEPS ([Wang et al., 2023](#bib.bib62)), and
JARVIS-1 ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib63)) use language-based planning.

Prior agents that solve long-horizon tasks thus depend on hand-crafted
rewards, expert video-action data, or both; Mirror instead only assumes
access to an expert-level video planner.

## 3 Method

![Refer to caption](2610.24177v1/exploration_intuition_v4.png)

Figure 1: Enabling long-horizon exploration with a video planner. Left:
Random exploration struggles to reach later stages of long-horizon tasks
that require specific sequences of actions. Right: The video planner
guides exploration. As the V2A model learns from achieved transitions,
the agent follows the plan more accurately and reaches progressively
later stages of the task. These new transitions further improve the
model, eventually enabling the agent to execute the full plan.

We seek a task-conditioned policy
$`\pi(a_{t}|o_{\leq t},l_{\mathtt{task}})`$, which predicts actions
$`a_{t}`$ based on past observations $`o_{\leq t}`$ and a task
$`l_{\mathtt{task}}`$. We model $`\pi`$ indirectly with two components:
a video planner (VP) and a video-to-action (V2A) model¹¹ 1 V2A models
are also commonly referred to as _inverse dynamics models (IDMs)_.. The
VP predicts future observations $`\hat{o}_{t+1}`$ based on historical
observations $`o_{\leq t}`$ and a task $`l_{\mathtt{task}}`$, while the
V2A model predicts actions $`a_{t}`$ given the combined video sequence
$`(o_{\leq t},\hat{o}_{t+1})`$. Sequentially sampling from the two
models yields the agent’s policy:

|     |                                                  |                                                                                                                                             |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle a*{t}\sim p*{\mathtt{V2A}}(\cdot | o*{\leq t},\hat{o}*{t+1})\quad\xleftarrow{\hskip 12.2917pt}\quad\hat{o}_{t+1}\sim p_{\mathtt{VP}}(\cdot\mid o*{\leq t},l*{\mathtt{task}})`$ |     |

Crucially, every plan is conditioned on the frames the agent _actually_
observed, never on its previous plans. The VP therefore always plans
from wherever the agent ended up, so deviations from earlier plans can
be corrected. For the same reason, errors do not compound over time,
which removes the need for anti-drift techniques against exposure bias
in autoregressive video generation ([Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib7);
[Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib71)).

This factorization differs from the world-model (WM) and policy
decomposition used by VLAs and world-model agents ([Hafner et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib19)), although both model the same joint distribution:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\begin{split}p(o_{t+1},a_{t}\mid o_{\leq t},l_{\mathtt{task}})&=\underbrace{p_{\mathtt{VP}}(o_{t+1}\mid o_{\leq t},l_{\mathtt{task}})}_{\text{action-free}}\times\underbrace{p_{\mathtt{V2A}}(a_{t}\mid o_{\leq t},o_{t+1})}_{\text{task-agnostic}}\\
&=\underbrace{p_{\mathtt{WM}}(o_{t+1}\mid o_{\leq t},a_{t})}_{\text{action-bound}}\times\underbrace{\pi(a_{t}\mid o_{\leq t},l_{\mathtt{task}})}_{\text{task-specific}}.\end{split}
``` |  | (1) |

The two decompositions differ in where the difficult reasoning is
learned. Long-horizon tasks require both procedural knowledge of what to
do and physical knowledge of how the world responds. In the WM + policy
decomposition, the policy must acquire the procedural knowledge and the
WM the action-conditioned physical knowledge, both from scarce,
embodiment-specific action data. In the VP + V2A decomposition, the VP
learns both from abundant action-free video, which enables web-scale
pretraining. This leaves the V2A model a much easier problem: a
task-agnostic mapping from observed transitions to actions. It therefore
needs far less embodiment-specific data, such as action labels. The
VP + V2A decomposition is thus considerably more scalable, as our
experiments
(Section [4.1.2](#S4.SS1.SSS2 "4.1.2 Self-improvement in Minecraft Survival Mode ‣ 4.1 Solving Long-Horizon Challenges in Minecraft ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models"))
and recent results in robot control ([Li et al., 2026](#bib.bib28))
show.

Our method, Mirror, reveals a far more striking consequence of this
decomposition: given a capable VP and the ability to interact with the
environment, the V2A model needs no action labels at all. Because it is
task-agnostic, it can learn from any transition the agent itself
produces, while the VP steers the agent toward the transitions the task
requires.
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Self-improving Video-to-Action Models ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")
shows how the V2A model can be trained from scratch on the data the
agent collects while following these plans, and
Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 A Video Planner for Online Learning and Closed-Loop Control ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")
describes how we make a generative video model VP practical for an
online agent.

Figure 2: Re-planning holds the agent at the milestone until noise
supplies the critical action.

### 3.1 Self-improving Video-to-Action Models

Our key insight is to use a pretrained video planner to guide data
collection for training the V2A model. The model learns from the agent’s
own rollouts, without expert action labels. As summarized in
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.1 Self-improving Video-to-Action Models ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models"),
training alternates between data collection and model updates. During
data collection, we sample an action from the agent’s two-stage policy
$`\pi`$ and add exploration noise $`n_{t}{\sim}\pi_{\mathtt{explore}}`$.
We execute the resulting action $`a_{t}`$ in the environment and store
the transition $`(o_{\leq t},a_{t},o_{t+1})`$ in a replay buffer. To
update the model, we sample batches from the buffer and train the V2A
model to predict $`a_{t}`$ from $`(o_{\leq t},o_{t+1})`$. Because the
targets are conditioned on the *achieved* observation $`o_{t+1}`$ rather
than the planned one $`\hat{o}_{t+1}`$, every transition is a valid
training example, even when execution deviates from the plan. Further
details can be found in
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.1 Self-improving Video-to-Action Models ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models").

video planner $`p_{\mathtt{VP}}`$, environment $`\mathcal{E}`$,
exploration distribution $`\pi_{\mathtt{explore}}`$, horizon $`T`$.

Initialize V2A model $`p_{\mathtt{V2A}}`$ with parameters $`\theta`$
from scratch; replay buffer $`\mathcal{D}\leftarrow\emptyset`$.

Repeat until convergence:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Algorithm 1 Learning without action labels: VP-guided self-training of
the V2A model

Exploration via stochastic V2A.
Figure [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")
illustrates how this process guides exploration. Early in training, the
V2A model often fails to follow the plan, so the realized next
observation $`o_{t+1}`$ may differ substantially from the video plan
$`\hat{o}_{t+1}`$. However, even these failed attempts provide useful
training examples: the V2A model still learns to predict the action that
produced the observed transition. As the model improves, the agent can
follow the planner more closely and reach later stages of the task. In
turn, these rollouts provide data to improve the V2A model at the newly
reached stages. Repeating this cycle allows the agent to progress ever
further through the task. In contrast, purely random exploration often
struggles to reach these stages because they require long sequences of
consistently coordinated actions.

If the V2A model were trained only on data from its own rollouts, it
would collapse to predicting the same action regardless of the
observations. We hence make the V2A model stochastic during data
collection by adding noise to its predictions. Stochasticity also plays
a second, central role: carrying the agent past the stages it cannot yet
execute
(Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")).
Where the V2A model is already competent, action noise is harmless:
while the agent may drift off the currently active video plan, the video
planner re-plans from the state actually reached, preventing error
accumulation and allowing the agent to progress. At a milestone the V2A
model has not yet learned, such as the first time a block has to be
mined, the V2A model predicts the wrong action, and the agent thus fails
to produce the planned transition. The planner, however, continues
re-planning, repeatedly proposing the same transition. A deterministic
agent would then be blocked at this milestone, as it would have never
seen the action that would lead to this correct transition. The
stochastic V2A model is what overcomes the roadblock: eventually, the
correct random action is sampled, and the resulting transition enters
the replay buffer (where it is then learned by the V2A model), enabling
the agent to complete the milestone in future episodes. Random
exploration, in contrast, would first have to stumble upon the entire
action sequence leading to the milestone before it could even attempt
the critical action, see
Fig. [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models").

![Refer to caption](2610.24177v1/VP_arch.png)

Figure 3: The causal video planner. (a) Tokenized frames and text are
fed into the 14B-parameter Cosmos3-Nano ([NVIDIA, 2026](#bib.bib43))
model, forming a causal stream of contexts whose keys and values are
cached and reused. The denoiser generates $`K`$ future frames while
cross-attending to the context KV cache, so each observation and
instruction is encoded only once. (b) Attention mask. Video history is
encoded block-causally. The future plan attends to this history and
bidirectionally to itself. Sliding-window attention lets the planner
generalize beyond the window while keeping the KV cache within a
constant budget.

### 3.2 A Video Planner for Online Learning and Closed-Loop Control

Following plans in closed-loop places three demands on the VP. First, it
must re-plan often and cheaply. Second, it must run over long episodes,
often well over a minute in our Minecraft benchmarks. Third, it must
stay on task even when the agent’s failures push it off the distribution
of expert videos. To avoid re-encoding the history at every re-plan, we
use a block-causal architecture: each observed frame is encoded once to
cache its keys and values while the plan is denoised bidirectionally
against this cache. Sliding-window attention over a fixed-size cache
keeps the cost per plan constant, so a planner trained on 32 s clips can
run on over 5 minutes of context without degradation. Finally, we
propose task-aware guidance, which leverages diffusion guidance ([Ho &
Salimans, 2022](#bib.bib21); [Karras et al., 2024](#bib.bib24)) to guide
the task-conditional video planner with a task-unconditional one,
significantly improving the planner’s task adherence.
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 Self-improving Video-to-Action Models ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")
and
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Video Planner ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")
detail the architecture, training, and inference.

## 4 Experiments

We empirically validate Mirror’s ability to solve tasks across Minecraft
(Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Solving Long-Horizon Challenges in Minecraft ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models"))
and traditional RL environments
(Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Solving Robotics Tasks and Video Games ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")).
In
Section [4.1.3](#S4.SS1.SSS3 "4.1.3 Emergent Capabilities of the Video Planner ‣ 4.1 Solving Long-Horizon Challenges in Minecraft ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models"),
we study what emergent abilities generative video planners can provide
with scale and how to leverage them. In
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Solving Robotics Tasks and Video Games ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models"),
we investigate how our method generalizes to various environments and
control settings. Please find video results on our
[website.](https://wilcoxsonm21.github.io/mirror/)

### 4.1 Solving Long-Horizon Challenges in Minecraft

Mirror solves long-horizon challenges in Minecraft without reward
supervision or expert actions. On Minecraft, we pre-train a video
planner on 2,946 hours of videos from the VPT dataset ([Baker et al.,
2022](#bib.bib3)), equipping our video planner with general physical and
procedural knowledge of Minecraft. The VP is finetuned further for
BASALT and Minecraft survival mode. With this VP, we are able to train
our self-improving V2A model from scratch with self-play. Our agent
operates in the MineRL 1.0 ([Guss et al., 2019](#bib.bib17)) action
space: at every step (20 Hz), it chooses among over 4,000 distinct
combinations of 20 keyboard buttons while moving the mouse continuously
in two dimensions. We do not simplify the action space or game
mechanics.

#### 4.1.1 Learning to Solve Fuzzy Tasks from Human Demonstration

We first evaluate Mirror on the Minecraft BASALT (Benchmark for Agents
that Solve Almost-Lifelike Tasks) ([Shah et al., 2021](#bib.bib52))
challenge. Unlike traditional RL environments, its task objectives are
intentionally fuzzy and hard-to-verify. For instance, consider the
MakeWaterfall task:

> Place a water bucket to make a beautiful waterfall. Then take an
> aesthetic picture of it by moving to a good location, positioning the
> player to have a nice view of the waterfall.

Our method is particularly suited to this kind of task where reward
specification is difficult. It learns directly from fuzzy human
demonstration videos without any reward supervision. For each task, we
finetune our video planner on the corresponding BASALT human video
demonstrations. We then train our V2A model from scratch only via
self-play. After only 5 hours (360,000 environment steps) of in-game
play, our method is already able to outperform the baselines.
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1.1 Learning to Solve Fuzzy Tasks from Human Demonstration ‣ 4.1 Solving Long-Horizon Challenges in Minecraft ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")
demonstrates how Mirror solves these tasks. Using the same VP, we also
evaluate a V2A model pretrained on expert actions from the VPT dataset.

In
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1.1 Learning to Solve Fuzzy Tasks from Human Demonstration ‣ 4.1 Solving Long-Horizon Challenges in Minecraft ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models"),
we compare our method against an action free baseline,
VIPER ([Escontrela et al., 2023](#bib.bib12)), a behavioral cloning (BC)
policy fine-tuned from VPT, action-supervised methods and heuristic
methods from the BASALT challenge ([Milani et al., 2022](#bib.bib38)),
and vision-language-action (VLA) Minecraft models: STEVE-1 ([Lifshitz
et al., 2023](#bib.bib31)), GROOT ([Cai et al., 2024](#bib.bib6)),
JARVIS-VLA ([Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib27)), OpenHA ([Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib64)). Of the BASALT challenge submissions, KAIROS is an
inverse RL method based on IQ-Learn ([Garg et al., 2021](#bib.bib15)),
UniTeam augments the VPT BC policy with search, and GoUp executes
pre-programmed scripts ([Milani et al., 2022](#bib.bib38)).

Even without expert actions, Mirror outperforms all baselines that do
not rely on hand-crafted heuristics. Only 5 hours of self-play were
required to achieve the highest success rate on FindCave and
MakeWaterfall tasks. To the best of our knowledge, Mirror is the first
method to achieve non-zero success on MakeWaterfall from learned
behavior alone (i.e., without classifiers or hard-coded actions). The
baselines fail in different ways
(Figure [18](#A3.F18 "Figure 18 ‣ C.3 Individual Task Learning Curves for Robotics and Atari ‣ Appendix C Additional Results ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")):
the action-supervised methods (KAIROS, BC and UniTeam) drift out of
distribution on multi-step tasks such as MakeWaterfall, the VLA models
struggle to follow the task descriptions, and GoUp’s hard-coded scripts
are brittle, placing, for instance, the water bucket but freezing once
underwater, whereas Mirror escapes the water using knowledge learned
from human gameplay. CreateAnimalPen and BuildVillageHouse remain
unsolved by all learning-based methods. Lastly, while Mirror does not
require action labels, it can still leverage them for a further small
performance gain.

#### 4.1.2 Self-improvement in Minecraft Survival Mode

We next evaluate Mirror on the Minecraft Diamond Challenge ([Guss
et al., 2019](#bib.bib17)), in which the agent must obtain a diamond in
survival mode, starting from a new world and an empty inventory. In the
online setting, Mirror is the first method to acquire an iron pickaxe
through self-improvement alone, without reward supervision or expert
action labels. In the offline setting, where expert action labels are
available but environment interaction is not, Mirror obtains diamonds at
nearly eight times the success rate of Dreamer V4 ([Hafner et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib19)), the state-of-the-art world-model agent on Minecraft
(Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Self-improvement with a generative VP. ‣ 4.1.2 Self-improvement in Minecraft Survival Mode ‣ 4.1 Solving Long-Horizon Challenges in Minecraft ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")).

Unlike the BASALT tasks, the Diamond Challenge has an unambiguous and
easily verifiable objective, but reaching it requires an extremely long
horizon of up to an hour of gameplay. The agent must complete a long
chain of prerequisite subgoals, from chopping trees and crafting tools
to smelting iron and mining deep underground. While our video planner
alone can solve the 3–5-minute BASALT tasks without any task
decomposition
(Sec. [4.1.1](#S4.SS1.SSS1 "4.1.1 Learning to Solve Fuzzy Tasks from Human Demonstration ‣ 4.1 Solving Long-Horizon Challenges in Minecraft ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")),
an hour-long horizon remains beyond it. Such a horizon is hard even for
humans: players given 20 minutes to obtain a diamond pickaxe collect
diamonds in only 15% of episodes ([Baker et al., 2022](#bib.bib3)).

To solve such an extremely long-horizon task, we follow Dreamer V4 and
condition the agent on its current subgoal. Whereas Dreamer V4
conditions its policy on one-hot task embeddings, we instead condition
only the video planner: we finetune it on subgoal intervals of VPT human
gameplay with text prompts that describe the subgoal. During rollouts, a
heuristic subgoal task planner chooses the prompt from the player’s own
state, namely the inventory, the health, and whether a GUI screen is
open. The V2A model therefore never observes the subgoal. Since
Dreamer V4 publishes neither how it extracts subgoal intervals from the
VPT recordings nor how it decides when to advance to the next subgoal
during evaluation, we implement our own data curation
(Appendix [B.1.4](#A2.SS1.SSS4 "B.1.4 Diamond Video Planner Data ‣ B.1 Minecraft ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details and Baseline Selection ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models"))
and heuristic subgoal task planner
(Appendix [B.1.5](#A2.SS1.SSS5 "B.1.5 Subgoal Task Planner ‣ B.1 Minecraft ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details and Baseline Selection ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")).

##### Video planning with a pretrained V2A model.

To study the video planner independently of the self-improvement
algorithm, we first evaluate it with a V2A model pretrained on 3k hours
of paired human action-demonstration data from the VPT dataset ([Baker
et al., 2022](#bib.bib3)). In this offline setting, our agent sets a new
state of the art, obtaining a diamond in 5.5% of episodes, compared with
0.7% for Dreamer 4 ([Hafner et al., 2025b](#bib.bib19)), the best
world-model agent. This supports the VP + V2A decomposition
in equation [1](#S3.E1 "In 3 Method ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")
over WM + policy decompositions such as Dreamer 4’s. A WM + policy agent
must learn procedural and physical knowledge from action-labeled data,
whereas the VP learns both from internet-scale video. Vision-language
pretraining does not supply this knowledge either: the Gemma 3-based
VLA ([Team, 2025](#bib.bib55)) evaluated by [Hafner et al.
(2025b)](#bib.bib19) never obtains a diamond.

##### Self-improvement with a generative VP.

Without action labels or rewards, our self-improving V2A model matches
its supervised counterpart on early-game items and remains competitive
with offline methods trained on 2.5k hours of action-labeled
demonstrations. We begin self-improvement with a V2A model trained from
scratch and a goal to acquire wood. While the V2A model may output
random actions early in training, re-planning allows the agent to
recover from its mistakes so it remains in distribution. Once the agent
succeeds at a goal, the text prompt is updated with the next goal. The
agent thus collects progressively more challenging items through online
interaction.
Appendix [B.1.6](#A2.SS1.SSS6 "B.1.6 Diamond V2A Training ‣ B.1 Minecraft ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details and Baseline Selection ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")
details the exploration strategy and the training protocol. After 140
hours of online interaction (about 10M environment steps), our agent
crafts a stone pickaxe in 72.7% of episodes and an iron pickaxe in
15.6%. At the same budget, Dreamer V3 ([Hafner et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib18)) crafts an iron pickaxe in only 1.7% of episodes,
despite using task rewards, simplified crafting, and accelerated mining
(Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Self-improvement with a generative VP. ‣ 4.1.2 Self-improvement in Minecraft Survival Mode ‣ 4.1 Solving Long-Horizon Challenges in Minecraft ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")).
Mirror retains a large margin even when matching Dreamer V3’s evaluation
protocol
(Appendix [C.1.3](#A3.SS1.SSS3 "C.1.3 Diamond Challenge under the Dreamer V3 Protocol ‣ C.1 Minecraft ‣ Appendix C Additional Results ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")),
in which episodes last 30 minutes and end at the first death, rather
than the 60-minute episodes with respawning used by VPT ([Baker et al.,
2022](#bib.bib3)) and Dreamer V4 ([Hafner et al., 2025b](#bib.bib19)).

##### Self-improvement with an oracle VP.

Generative video planners are already capable, and we expect them to
keep improving. To examine how Mirror scales with better planners, we
decouple self-improvement from the generative VP using an oracle video
planner (oracle VP), which we construct from an expert policy and a copy
of the environment. At each planning step, we synchronize a separate
instance of the game to the agent’s current state and let the expert
policy, conditioned on the agent’s past observations $`o_{\leq t}`$,
play forward in it. The frames rendered by this copy serve as the plan
$`\hat{o}_{t+1}`$, so the oracle has the same input-output behavior as a
video planner, $`p_{\tt{VP}}(\hat{o}_{t+1}\mid o_{\leq t})`$, while the
expert’s actions are never shown to the V2A model.

Using VPT’s early-game RL policy ([Baker et al., 2022](#bib.bib3)) as
the oracle, we train a V2A model from scratch with self-play. After only
about 80 hours of online interaction, the agent acquires diamonds for
the first time
(Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Self-improvement with a generative VP. ‣ 4.1.2 Self-improvement in Minecraft Survival Mode ‣ 4.1 Solving Long-Horizon Challenges in Minecraft ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")),
an order of magnitude fewer environment interactions than
Dreamer V3 ([Hafner et al., 2025a](#bib.bib18)) requires, despite
Dreamer V3’s use of simplified crafting and accelerated mining. RL
agents take far longer because they must explore the full action space
on their own. This experiment suggests that the remaining bottleneck is
not Mirror’s ability to learn from interaction, but the capability of
the video planner itself.

![Refer to caption](2610.24177v1/text-conditioned-paths.png)

Figure 7: Text-conditioned video planning. We evaluate text-conditioned
control on 10 tasks across two unseen environments (see
Appendix [C.1.4](#A3.SS1.SSS4 "C.1.4 Text-Conditioned Minecraft Evaluation ‣ C.1 Minecraft ‣ Appendix C Additional Results ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")).
Each task is specified only through a text prompt, with no task-specific

as a reward-free video-based baseline. Combined with our self-improving

Training the video planner on internet-scale video data unlocks novel
capabilities without requiring additional fine-tuning for each task. We
explore such emergent behaviors in two settings.

##### Emergent in-context learning from failure.

We examine if Mirror can utilize its history, $`o_{\leq t}`$, for
in-context learning. In
Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.1.3 Emergent Capabilities of the Video Planner ‣ 4.1 Solving Long-Horizon Challenges in Minecraft ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models"),
we challenge our agent to escape a lava lake. If the agent falls in the
lava, it respawns at the origin. We compare a case where the agent’s
history is preserved between deaths, and a case when the history is
reset after every death. The task is difficult: with fresh histories
every life, the escape rate is only 3%. When video context is retained
between lives, however, the agent leverages its past failures to improve
its escape rate.
Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.1.3 Emergent Capabilities of the Video Planner ‣ 4.1 Solving Long-Horizon Challenges in Minecraft ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")
(b) shows the resulting agent’s trajectories. With shared history, the
agent exhibits a clear directional bias, demonstrating that prior
attempts influence the agent’s behavior. With independent history, the
agent moves in relatively uniform directions around the starting point.
Retaining history does not provide a comparable benefit to the VPT BC
policy, perhaps even hindering performance. This experiment shows that
our video planning agent exhibits some emergent in-context adaptation.

##### Text-conditioned video planning.

As a proof of concept, we test whether our pretrained video planner can
be steered by text zero-shot. Since our planner was trained only on
captions generated automatically by a small VLM
(Appendix [A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 Caption Generation ‣ Appendix A Video Planner ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")),
we evaluate simple goals such as “chop down the tree” or “dig into the
ground,” rather than complex instructions. Accordingly, we do not aim to
compete in language understanding with Minecraft-specialized
vision-language-action models such as JARVIS-VLA ([Li et al.,
2025](#bib.bib27)) and OpenHA ([Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib64)). Each
task nevertheless lasts about 30 seconds and requires consistent,
prolonged behavior. We pair the text-conditioned video planner with a
V2A model pre-trained on random walks, a V2A model pre-trained on the
VPT expert actions, and our self-improving V2A model. We also compare
against VIPER ([Escontrela et al., 2023](#bib.bib12)), which similarly
does not use action labels, and a text-conditioned BC policy
(Appendix [C.1.4](#A3.SS1.SSS4 "C.1.4 Text-Conditioned Minecraft Evaluation ‣ C.1 Minecraft ‣ Appendix C Additional Results ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")).
As shown in
Figure [7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 4.1.3 Emergent Capabilities of the Video Planner ‣ 4.1 Solving Long-Horizon Challenges in Minecraft ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models"),
Mirror reliably harvests trees, climbs hills, and digs underground,
although some tasks remain difficult across all V2A variants. The
self-improving V2A model generally outperforms the one trained on random
walks and remains competitive with the one supervised on human actions.
These results show that the V2A model can execute plans without ever
knowing the task. Since the V2A model is task-agnostic, a sufficiently
capable video planner would let the agent solve new tasks from a text
prompt alone, without task-specific action data or retraining.

### 4.2 Solving Robotics Tasks and Video Games

Setup. We evaluate Mirror on standard subsets of key synthetic
decision-making benchmarks: OGBench ([Park et al., 2025a](#bib.bib46)),
DeepMindControl ([Tassa et al., 2018](#bib.bib54)), and
Atari ([Bellemare et al., 2013](#bib.bib4); [Escontrela et al.,
2023](#bib.bib12)). We benchmark with BCO ([Torabi et al.,
2018](#bib.bib58)), which alternates between learning a V2A on policy
rollouts and cloning its inferred actions on expert demonstrations,
VIPER ([Escontrela et al., 2023](#bib.bib12)), which uses video
prediction likelihoods as rewards, LAIfO ([Giammarino et al.,
2024](#bib.bib16)), which learns a policy by adversarially matching
expert and agent transitions, and the method proposed by [Luo & Du
(2024)](#bib.bib36) (which we abbreviate as “Grounding”) which learns a
goal-conditioned policy to reach video-predicted subgoals. We evaluate
Mirror with both a learned video planner and an oracle planner that
supplies future frames from an RL expert. Unlike in our Minecraft
setting, large-scale human play datasets are not available, and we thus
found it essential to augment the generative planner’s training data
with recovery examples collected using DAgger ([Ross et al.,
2011](#bib.bib49)). Please find an in-depth discussion of dataset
construction, evaluated tasks, planner training, and baseline
implementations in Appendix
[B](#A2 "Appendix B Implementation Details and Baseline Selection ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models").

Generative VP results. As shown in
Figure [8](#S4.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Text-conditioned video planning. ‣ 4.1.3 Emergent Capabilities of the Video Planner ‣ 4.1 Solving Long-Horizon Challenges in Minecraft ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models"),
among methods evaluated without oracle planners, Mirror surpasses all
baselines on Atari and OGBench, and learns faster than LAIfO on DMC.
LAIfO performs less consistently across domains, learning less
efficiently on OGBench and achieving limited returns on Atari. VIPER
also achieves low returns on Atari, suggesting that using video model
predictions directly provides better supervision than likelihood-based
rewards.

The comparisons with BCO and Grounding help explain these gains.
Although BCO also learns a V2A model from self-collected experience, it
performs substantially worse, indicating the importance of using the
video planner to guide data collection. Grounding improves on BCO,
consistent with the benefit of video-guided exploration, but still
remains substantially below Mirror. The remaining gap suggests an
advantage to learning a V2A model that translates frame-to-frame
transitions into actions over learning a goal-conditioned policy to
reach predicted subgoals.

Oracle VP results. To evaluate our self-improvement algorithm
independently of video-planner quality, we also use an Oracle VP that
supplies frames from an RL expert. In this setting, our method matches
the expert on Atari, suggesting that our Atari performance is limited by
the video planner, most likely by the compute needed to train a model
that accurately predicts fine details such as the motion of small
projectiles. This result demonstrates that as video models continue to
scale and improve, our method provides a simple framework that is able
to solve a wide variety of tasks. In Appendix
[C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 OGBench Generalization Analysis ‣ Appendix C Additional Results ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models"),
we also demonstrate that Mirror learns a V2A model that generalizes
better to unseen goals.

Mirror also exceeds the expert’s return in Assault and Zaxxon by 10% and
25%, respectively. We observe that the expert issues redundant fire
commands that do not produce additional shots. The V2A model can thus
follow the plan without copying them. As a result, Mirror makes fewer
ineffective firing attempts in Assault, reducing overheating, and
releases FIRE more frequently in Zaxxon, enabling subsequent presses to
trigger new shots.

## 5 Conclusion

We have introduced Mirror, a method that learns to translate behaviors
encoded in large video planners to policies executable by an agent.
Unlike prior work, our method assumes neither paired video-action data
nor task-specific rewards, but instead learns to translate video into
actions simply by self-play in an interactive environment.

##### Limitations.

Our approach has several limitations. First, without a separate
high-level task planner that conditions the video planner on subgoals,
our agent could not cover the hour-long horizon of the diamond task. We
expect capable VLM-based task planners to fill this role in the future:
VLMs excel at abstract, high-level task planning but struggle with
dense, low-level control, whereas video planners show the opposite
strengths, making the two naturally complementary. Second, with
self-improvement alone, our agent reaches the iron pickaxe but does not
yet mine diamonds. An imperfect V2A model often leads the agent into
suboptimal states that human players rarely visit, and recovering from
them demands very strong generalization from the video planner. Our
video planner falls short of this at later milestones, each of which is
covered by only a few hours of human gameplay in our training data.
Third, some actions leave no visible trace, so inferring them from
vision alone and from scratch is ill-posed; in practice, we expect a
small amount of action data to resolve this. Lastly, training a capable
generative video planner can be data-intensive. Unlike human gameplay,
which naturally contains mistakes and recoveries, the data generated by
expert policies in our robotics and control benchmarks
(Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Solving Robotics Tasks and Video Games ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models"))
lacked diversity, so we needed to augment it with recovery data
collected via DAgger ([Ross et al., 2011](#bib.bib49)) to train a
sufficiently robust video planner.

We believe Mirror offers a promising path toward general-purpose agents
that acquire diverse behaviors from video pre-training and learn to
self-improve their execution through interaction.

## Appendix A Video Planner

##### Design principle.

The central goal behind the design of our video planner is long context.
Many of our tasks require memory over long horizons. Long context may
also help error recovery in closed-loop planning. Early in training, the
imperfect V2A model often deviates from expert behavior, forcing the
planner to operate on trajectories outside its training distribution.
With a short context, we often saw the planner repeat the same failed
behavior. With long context, we instead observed emergent recovery
behavior, as the planner can use its previous failures to change
strategy (see
Sec. [4.1.3](#S4.SS1.SSS3.Px1 "Emergent in-context learning from failure. ‣ 4.1.3 Emergent Capabilities of the Video Planner ‣ 4.1 Solving Long-Horizon Challenges in Minecraft ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models"))
and replan. This section describes how we make such long context
affordable.

### A.1 Architecture

Videos are encoded with the Wan2.2 VAE ([Wan Team, 2025](#bib.bib61)),
which compresses 4 frames in time and $`16\times 16`$ pixels in space
into 48 latent channels. The zeroth pixel frame is encoded on its own
rather than grouped with other frames, so $`L`$ latent frames correspond
to $`1+4(L-1)`$ pixel frames. The MineRL environment ([Baker et al.,
2022](#bib.bib3)) renders $`640\times 360`$ frames at 20 fps. We resize
each frame to $`320\times 192`$, so that every four-frame chunk (0.2 s)
is encoded into a $`12\times 20\times 48`$ latent array (height
$`\times`$ width $`\times`$ channels). A $`2\times 2`$ patchifier then
turns each latent frame into 60 tokens of 192 dimensions, which form the
input of the video planner.

##### Backbone.

The planner is initialized from Cosmos3-Nano ([NVIDIA,
2026](#bib.bib43)), a mixture of transformers ([Liang et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib30)) with a text tower and a video tower. The two towers
share the same Qwen3-VL ([Bai et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)) block design but
have separate weights. Each has 7B parameters, 36 layers of width 4096,
32q / 8kv GQA heads of dimension 128, SwiGLU MLPs of width 12,288. For
positional embedding, 3D-MROPE ([Su et al., 2024](#bib.bib53); [Bai
et al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [NVIDIA, 2026](#bib.bib43)) is used in which
the $`128`$-dim attention head is split into $`[48,24,24]`$-dims, each
encoding the time, height and width of the video. We freeze the text
tower and finetune only the video tower. The video tower plays two
roles: as a *context encoder*, it encodes the clean history of observed
frames, and as a *denoiser*, it denoises the frames of the plan. We
refer to the two roles separately for clarity, although they share the
same architecture and weights.

##### Block-sparse attention with FlexAttention.

The original Cosmos3 implementation uses NATTEN ([Hassani et al.,
2023](#bib.bib20)), which cannot efficiently express our block-causal
sliding-window attention pattern. We instead use FlexAttention ([Dong
et al., 2024](#bib.bib10)), which supports efficient attention with
arbitrary block-sparse masks. On NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, we
use FlexAttention’s experimental FlashAttention-4 ([Zadouri et al.,
2026](#bib.bib68)) backend, which is 1.35–1.55$`\times`$ faster than the
default Triton ([Tillet et al., 2019](#bib.bib57)) backend on our
workload. On AMD GPUs, we use the Triton backend.

##### Mixture-of-transformers attention.

In the original Cosmos3, all video tokens attend to each other
bidirectionally under a single mask. In our implementation, however, the
video tower’s role is split into a context encoder and a denoiser, which
require distinct attention patterns. The video history is block-causally
encoded frame by frame, whereas the future plans are jointly denoised
and thus require bidirectional attention. Together with the text, this
yields three token streams. At every layer, each stream self-attends to
its own tokens and cross-attends to the streams it is conditioned on:

- •
  Text (text tower): self-attends causally, token by token. It carries
  the video metadata (resolution, aspect ratio, duration and frame
  rate), which also serves as an attention sink, and optional task
  instructions.
- •
  History (context encoder): self-attends block-causally, i.e.,
  bidirectionally within a frame and causally across frames.
  Cross-attends to the text.
- •
  Plan (denoiser): self-attends bidirectionally within the plan.
  Cross-attends to the history and the text.

Handling all these attention patterns in a single joint attention would
require an overly complex attention mask. This is not only cumbersome to
implement but also substantially slows down the FlexAttention kernel. We
instead compute attention with a simpler mask for each source and merge
the results as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
o=\sum_{s}\frac{\exp(\mathrm{LSE}_{s})}{\sum_{s^{\prime}}\exp(\mathrm{LSE}_{s^{\prime}})}\,o_{s},
``` |  | (2) |

where the attention output $`o_{s}`$ and the log-sum-exp
$`\mathrm{LSE}_{s}`$ are computed separately for each source $`s`$. This
merge is mathematically equivalent to standard scaled dot-product
attention (SDPA) computed jointly over all sources. Keeping the sources
separate makes the implementation of variable-length training and cached
inference straightforward, at negligible overhead.

##### Attention sink.

In video models such as Wan ([Wan Team, 2025](#bib.bib61)), the zeroth
latent frame serves as the attention sink. In Cosmos3, whose
mixture-of-transformers structure lets every video token attend to the
text, the text tokens appear to play this role instead. Removing the
text tokens greatly slowed down the finetuning. Provided that every
video query can properly attend to the text metadata tokens, adapting
the pretrained bidirectional model to block-causal attention is fast,
taking fewer than 1,000 finetuning steps. On the other hand, removing
the zeroth latent frame from the attention context of the denoiser
caused only a small drop in performance if the history is long enough.
The sliding-window attention described below therefore does not keep the
zeroth latent frame; instead, every query always attends to the text.

##### Text conditioning format.

Our video planner is conditioned on two kinds of captions, written in
Cosmos3’s structured JSON format and wrapped in a chat template. Each
caption contains the video metadata (resolution, aspect ratio, duration
and frame rate) and, optionally, temporal information and language
instructions.

The context encoder takes a *task-level caption*, which describes the
long-horizon task sequence. It can optionally state how much time has
elapsed since the current task sequence began. We find that providing
this resume timestamp helps when the model context must be reset in the
middle of a task. The caption may also describe the preceding clip,
although we do not use this in our experiments. With all fields present,
it reads:

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

{"temporal_caption": "\<observations of the preceding 10 s\> The clip
resumes at 1:23.4. Task sequence: collect wood; then craft a crafting
table", "resolution": {"H": 192, "W": 320}, "aspect_ratio": "5,3",
"duration": "32.0s", "fps": 20}

The denoiser takes a *control-level caption*, which describes the
desired short-horizon behavior of the plan. The duration field is
included to help the denoiser handle variable-length prediction. It can
optionally state the time range of the plan to generate. An
unconditional plan uses the metadata-only caption.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,eyJhY3Rpb25zIjogW3sidGltZSI6ICIxOjI1LjAtMToyNi42IiwgImRlc2NyaXB0aW9uIjogIlBsYWNlIHRoZSBjcmFmdGluZyB0YWJsZSJ9XSwgInJlc29sdXRpb24iOiB7IkgiOiAxOTIsICJXIjogMzIwfSwgImFzcGVjdF9yYXRpbyI6ICI1LDMiLCAiZHVyYXRpb24iOiAiMS42cyIsICJmcHMiOiAyMH0=)

{"actions": \[{"time": "1:25.0-1:26.6", "description": "Place the
crafting table"}\], "resolution": {"H": 192, "W": 320}, "aspect_ratio":
"5,3", "duration": "1.6s", "fps": 20}

### A.2 Training

##### Objective.

We train with the linear interpolant $`x_{\tau}=(1-\tau)x+\tau\epsilon`$
and velocity prediction $`v=\epsilon-x`$ ([Lipman et al.,
2022](#bib.bib32); [Liu et al., 2022](#bib.bib34)), using a squared
error averaged over latent dimensions. Every target latent frame carries
equal weight in the loss. Following [Esser et al. (2024)](#bib.bib13)
and Wan ([Wan Team, 2025](#bib.bib61)), $`\tau`$ is drawn from a mixture
of a logit-normal distribution shifted towards higher noise scale. As
our plan resolution and length are smaller than those of typical video
models, we use relatively low shift. We use $`\mathtt{shift}=2`$ for VPT
pretraining and BASALT finetuning, and use $`3`$ for the diamond
finetuning. We also sample $`\tau`$ from a uniform distribution 10% of
the time to ensure better GUI interaction details and likelihood
estimation.

##### Variable plan length.

The right length for a plan is unknown in advance. Using too short plans
or planning autoregressively with the shortest chunk the VAE allows (one
latent frame, 0.2 s) produced poor plans, while 4 s is too long for
open-loop execution. We therefore train a single model on a mixture of
plan lengths from 0.2 s to 4 s. All frames of a prediction window share
one diffusion time, and different windows draw diffusion time and noise
independently. We also stochastically drop the text conditions of a
subset of the prediction windows for unconditional generation and
text-conditional classifier-free guidance ([Ho & Salimans,
2022](#bib.bib21)).

Each training sample is a 32 s video clip, which is block-causally
encoded as the clean history. Because this history is shared, we predict
many prediction windows from a single video clip at once. This reuse of
the context encoding is our key scaling knob. The learning signal comes
only from the denoised tokens, so predicting many windows per video clip
maximizes the learning signal per token. In our training setup, the
prediction windows of each video clip span twice its 32 s length,
totaling 64 s. Since the windows differ in position, length, diffusion
time and noise, predicting the same video clip twice still provides new
learning signal. In our gradient noise scale ([McCandlish et al.,
2018](#bib.bib37)) measurement at 30k steps, this double pass over a
video clip reduced the gradient noise as much as an additional fresh
video clip would. As the cost of encoding 32 s of history is amortized
over all windows of the video clip, long-context training becomes
affordable. Combined with sliding-window attention, this long-context
training lets the planner roll out far beyond the training length, to
about five minutes in our experiments.

Figure 9: Variable prediction length training. Prediction windows of
variable length over the same 32 s clip. The clean history is encoded
once by the context encoder and shared by all prediction windows. With
sliding-window attention, the clean history tokens and the noisy plan
windows attend to the preceding 12 s and 8 s clean frames, respectively.

##### Static shape training for variable-length plans.

Compiling every transformer block is essential for training speed, and
it requires static tensor shapes. FlexAttention makes this even more
important: its block mask is built for a specific sequence shape, so any
change of shape forces the mask and the attention kernel to be rebuilt
and recompiled. While FlexAttention also supports dynamic-shape
compilation, it is far less efficient than static compilation in both
throughput and memory. We therefore keep every tensor shape fixed for
training and express the variable prediction windows purely through the
attention mask. We illustrate this in
Figure [9](#A1.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Variable plan length. ‣ A.2 Training ‣ Appendix A Video Planner ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models").

In our setup, each GPU processes 6,144 text tokens for the frozen text
tower and one 32 s video clip as a fixed-length sequence of 9,600 clean
video tokens (160 latent frames $`\times`$ 60 tokens), followed by
19,200 noisy plan tokens. All three numbers are multiples of
FlexAttention’s 128-token block size, so the sequences align exactly
with the $`128\times 128`$ attention blocks for best efficiency. The
number, lengths and positions of the prediction windows change at every
step, but they only change the values of the boolean and integer
window/frame id tensors that the mask function reads. The mask function
for the video self-attention is:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathtt{attend}(q,k)=\big[\,k\text{ is clean}\;\wedge\;k\in\mathtt{SWA}(q)\,\big]\;\vee\;\big[\,q,k\text{ are noisy}\;\wedge\;\mathtt{plan\_id}(q)=\mathtt{plan\_id}(k)\,\big],`$ |  |

where $`\mathtt{SWA}(q)`$ is the set of clean tokens in the sliding
window of $`q`$. For a clean query, this is the preceding 12 s up to and
including its own frame. For a noisy query, this corresponds to the 8 s
of clean frames immediately before its prediction window.
$`\mathtt{plan\_id}(q)`$ is the index of the prediction window
containing $`q`$. We use $`\mathtt{plan\_id}(q)=0`$ for clean tokens.

##### Parallelism and memory.

We shard the video tower with Hybrid Sharded Data Parallel (HSDP)
strategy on multiple nodes using Pytorch FSDP2 library ([Zhao et al.,
2023b](#bib.bib70)). Parameters are sharded within each 8-GPU node and
replicated across nodes. We use activation checkpointing ([Chen et al.,
2016](#bib.bib9)) for each transformer block. On AMD MI350X GPUs (288 GB
of memory) we do not use activation checkpointing.

##### Precision.

We use BF16 precision for the computation. FSDP2 automatically downcasts
the FP32 weights to BF16. The gradients are reduced across ranks in
FP32. Numerically sensitive parts stay in FP32: the input patch
projection, the timestep embedder, the velocity head, RMS/LayerNorm, the
rotary embeddings, and the LSE attention merge. Training losses are
computed in double precision. The frozen text tower and the VAE run in
BF16. For pretraining, we additionally use FP8 mixed precision training
with dynamic tensorwise scaling for the linear layers. Because we use
sliding window attention (SWA), which is computed by an efficient
block-sparse kernel, the training step is dominated by these matrix
multiplications: FP8 speeds them up by about 1.6$`\times`$ and a full
training step by about 1.3$`\times`$. We found no evidence that FP8
training degrades the planning quality. FP8 can be disabled for cooldown
or finetuning to reach a lower loss floor.

##### Optimization and pretraining schedule.

We use AdamW ([Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017](#bib.bib35)) with
$`\beta=(0.9,0.95)`$, $`\epsilon=10^{-8}`$ and weight decay 0.01, a
1,000-step linear warm-up followed by a constant learning rate, gradient
clipping at global norm 3.0, and an EMA of the weights with decay
0.9999. We chose AdamW because Cosmos3 was trained with it. We
pretrained on VPT contractor dataset ([Baker et al., 2022](#bib.bib3))
for 220k steps. As GPUs became available we grew the global batch from 8
to 32, raising the learning rate roughly with the square root of the
batch size
(Table [2](#A1.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Optimization and pretraining schedule. ‣ A.2 Training ‣ Appendix A Video Planner ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")),
and ended with a 5k-step cooldown at a constant $`5\times 10^{-6}`$. The
run took roughly 4,700 H200 GPU-hours of training steps. The final
pretrain checkpoint is the step-220k EMA.

| Steps | GPUs | Global batch | Learning rate | Wall-clock |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| 0–30k | 8 H200 | 8 | $`1.5\times 10^{-5}`$ | 25 h |
| 30k–80k | 16 H200 (2 nodes) | 16 | $`2.0\times 10^{-5}`$ | 42 h |
| 80k–215k | 32 H200 (4 nodes) | 32 | $`2.7\times 10^{-5}`$ | 115 h |
| 215k–220k | 8 H200 | 32 | $`5\times 10^{-6}`$ (cooldown) | 10 h |

Table 2: Pretraining schedule of the video planner on VPT dataset.

##### Pretraining data.

The VPT contractor dataset contains 2,945.7 hours of gameplay. We
excluded one game-version subset (6.9; 271 recordings, 21.8 h) whose
logged cursor coordinates are malformed; the coordinates are needed
because the recordings do not show the cursor inside menus, so we draw
it back into those frames. We also excluded low-quality data (7.9 h),
leaving 55,919 recordings (2,916.0 h) for training. Training samples a
recording uniformly and then a random 32 s clip from it. Frames are
resized from $`640\times 360`$ to $`320\times 192`$ with bilinear
interpolation and antialiasing. Over 220k steps, the planner saw about
98,000 hours of noisy video clips. The captions are generated from the
videos with the Cosmos3-Nano VLM, as described in
Appendix [A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 Caption Generation ‣ Appendix A Video Planner ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models").

##### Finetuning.

The pretrained video planner is finetuned for each downstream task with
global batch 8 (16 to 32 for the Diamond planners) and an EMA decay of
0.9995. The number of steps varies from 10k to 50k depending on the task
difficulty and the amount of available video data. The BASALT planners
are trained only on human gameplay videos, without text instructions,
with a learning rate of $`10^{-5}`$, a 1k-step warm-up and cosine decay.
BASALT episodes end when the player presses the Esc button, which is not
visible in the video. We therefore finetune the video planner to predict
a gray screen once the player presses the Esc button. The Diamond
planners were finetuned with 16 MI350X GPUs on our curated split of
human VPT gameplay, divided into subgoal clips
(Appendix [B.1.4](#A2.SS1.SSS4 "B.1.4 Diamond Video Planner Data ‣ B.1 Minecraft ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details and Baseline Selection ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")).
Text conditioning informs the planner of the current stage of the
diamond tech tree.

### A.3 Inference

Figure 10: Rolling cache at inference. (1) Each new observation is
encoded once by the context encoder, which attends to the 12 s cache.
(2) The resulting keys and values are appended and the oldest context is
evicted, keeping the cache size fixed. (3) The denoiser generates the
next 1.6 s of video while attending to the last 8 s of cached context
and, optionally, to a control-level caption. Cache cells schematically
group frames.

##### Rolling cache with a fixed budget.

At inference, the planner keeps the keys and values of only the most
recent 12 s of observations in a fixed-size ring-buffer cache. Each
newly observed frame is encoded once by the context encoder using this
cache. This new frame replaces the oldest frame in the cache, which no
query can attend to anymore because of the sliding window. To plan, the
denoiser generates the next 1.6 s future by attending to the last 8 s of
the cache and optionally to the control-level caption. Because the cache
size never grows, every plan costs the same and the model can be
compiled with static shape. We illustrate this in
Figure [10](#A1.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ A.3 Inference ‣ Appendix A Video Planner ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models").

##### Sampling.

Plans are sampled with the second-order UniPC solver ([Zhao et al.,
2023a](#bib.bib69)) for 20 steps with a time shift of 3. We quantize the
linear layers of the video tower to FP8 with per-tensor dynamic scaling,
which makes planning $`1.43\times`$ faster than BF16 on an H200. With 20
solver steps and autoguidance, the planner generates about 4.2 s of
video per second of computation on a single H200.

##### Task-aware guidance.

We use two forms of task-aware guidance. For the BASALT tasks, we use a
variant of autoguidance ([Karras et al., 2024](#bib.bib24)), where the
positive model is the finetuned planner and the negative model is a
planner trained on broader, less task-specific data, such as its parent
before task finetuning; we use a guidance scale of 1.5. For
Sec. [4.1.3](#S4.SS1.SSS3.Px2 "Text-conditioned video planning. ‣ 4.1.3 Emergent Capabilities of the Video Planner ‣ 4.1 Solving Long-Horizon Challenges in Minecraft ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")
and
Sec. [4.1.2](#S4.SS1.SSS2 "4.1.2 Self-improvement in Minecraft Survival Mode ‣ 4.1 Solving Long-Horizon Challenges in Minecraft ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models"),
we use text classifier-free guidance ([Ho & Salimans, 2022](#bib.bib21))
with a scale of 7. For
Sec. [4.1.2](#S4.SS1.SSS2 "4.1.2 Self-improvement in Minecraft Survival Mode ‣ 4.1 Solving Long-Horizon Challenges in Minecraft ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models"),
the text consists of one of 16 subgoal captions from log to diamond,
chosen by the subgoal task planner
(Appendix [B.1.5](#A2.SS1.SSS5 "B.1.5 Subgoal Task Planner ‣ B.1 Minecraft ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details and Baseline Selection ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")).
The conditional and unconditional branches share the cached history, so
guidance doubles only the denoiser’s computation. We find that
task-aware guidance is crucial for goal persistence. Without it, the
planner often abandons the current goal after repeated failures. As a
result, it may skip necessary steps and move on to the next subgoal
before completing the current one. Task-aware classifier-free guidance
effectively suppresses repeated mistakes and strengthens adherence to
the intended goal.

### A.4 Caption Generation

##### Pipeline.

We captioned the VPT corpus with the vision-language model of
Cosmos3-Nano ([NVIDIA, 2026](#bib.bib43)), served offline by vLLM ([Kwon
et al., 2023](#bib.bib26)) with JSON-schema-constrained decoding
(temperature 0.7, top-$`p`$ 0.8, top-$`k`$ 20). We aim for text that is
both *descriptive*, grounded in what is visible, and *instructional*,
phrased the way a user would command an agent. We therefore generate
captions in three stages. A strictly factual stage comes first, and
later stages only rephrase or group its output.

1.  1.
    *Descriptions.* The model watches overlapping windows of every video
    at four temporal scales. These are 8 s windows every 4 s at 4 fps,
    24 s windows every 12 s at 1 fps, and 64 s windows every 32 s at
    0.5 fps, all at $`192\times 320`$. The fourth scale is short windows
    at full $`640\times 360`$ resolution centered on salient moments
    (attacks, opening a menu, jumps, sharp turns, climbs and descents of
    at least four blocks). The model is not told why a window was
    chosen. The model lists up to six atomic, intent-free descriptions
    per window, each with a start and end time.
2.  2.
    *Instructions.* Batches of 40 descriptions, together with the video
    covering their time span, are rewritten one-to-one into imperative
    instructions. Each instruction inherits the description’s time span.
3.  3.
    *Tasks.* From the video duration and up to 110 descriptions evenly
    distributed across time, the model partitions the whole recording
    into 1–8 consecutive task segments and infers the intent that makes
    each segment’s behavior coherent. We run this stage five times per
    video with different seeds, which yields five alternative task
    partitions.

The description stage took 4.6 hours on 32 H200 GPUs, plus 1.2 hours for
the coarsest scale.

##### Prompts.

The instructions of the three stages, verbatim:

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

This is a clip from a Minecraft gameplay recording; each frame is
preceded by its \<t seconds\> timestamp within the full episode. List
the distinct things the player OBSERVABLY does, as separate facts. For
each fact give start_s and end_s in those same episode seconds, read
from the frame timestamps. Rules: describe only what is visible on
screen --- never goals, purposes or attempts (no ’trying to’, ’in order
to’, ’prepares to’, ’searching for’); one atomic action or event per
fact; repeated actions separated in time are separate facts; name
blocks/items/mobs/GUI screens concretely when identifiable (hotbar,
inventory, crafting table, crosshair target); 6-20 words per fact. If
nothing notable happens, return one fact describing the ongoing state
(movement direction, terrain).

Stage 1: descriptions (system: “You are a helpful assistant.”; input:
video)

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Below are OBSERVATIONS of what a Minecraft player did, each on its own
line with an index. Rewrite EVERY observation as a CONTROL: the
instruction a coach could have given just before it, which that
behaviour then obeys.

Rules for each control:

- Imperative, 3-14 words, concrete Minecraft vocabulary. Command the
ACTION, not the scene: ’Mine the coal seam in the left wall’, not ’The
player mines coal’.

- Say only what the observation says. Add no goals, no reasons, no
purpose clauses (’to get wood’, ’so that...’), no outcomes the player
could not know in advance.

- A coach speaks before the fact, so drop discoveries and results from
the wording: ’Open the furnace’ rather than ’Open the furnace, revealing
an iron ingot’.

- Keep the affirmative form; never write ’Don’t’, ’Avoid’ or ’Stop’.

- Return one control per index, for every index given, in the same
order.

Stage 2: instructions (system: “You are a precise Minecraft gameplay
annotator.”; input: video + indexed descriptions)

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

You are splitting one Minecraft recording into its TASKS.

A TASK answers exactly one question:

What ongoing purpose makes this stretch of the trajectory coherent?

It is NOT a summary of what happened in order.

BAD (activity summary): "Walks around, gathers wood, opens the
inventory, and mines."

GOOD (intent hypothesis): "Prepare equipment for underground
exploration."

The segments run back to back and together they cover the WHOLE
recording, from the

first frame to the last. You give only the END of each segment: the
first starts at

0 s, every later one starts where the previous ended, and the last one
ends at the

video duration. Give the ends in increasing order.

Rules:

- A segment should normally cover at least 30 seconds.

- Split where the player’s PURPOSE changes, not where the scenery
changes.

- Name the intent that makes each whole segment coherent, in 6-20 words
of concrete

Minecraft vocabulary, grounded in the facts.

- Do not add narrative detail the evidence does not support.

- Cite the fact ids that support each segment.

VIDEO DURATION: \<duration\> s

FACTS (intent-neutral observations, video-relative seconds):

\[f12\] 3.0-5.5s \<observation\>

...

Return the JSON object with your segments.

Stage 3: tasks (system: “You are a precise annotator of MINECRAFT
gameplay. Every session, task and control below comes from a recording
of a human playing Minecraft, and every word you write must be Minecraft
vocabulary.”; input: text only)

##### Filtering.

We clean the generated captions with simple rules:

- •
  decoding is constrained to a JSON schema;
- •
  description times are clamped to their window;
- •
  empty or zero-length items are dropped, 1.5% of descriptions in the
  rewrite;
- •
  task boundaries are closed into an exact partition on the frame clock.

##### Statistics.

Table [3](#A1.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Statistics. ‣ A.4 Caption Generation ‣ Appendix A Video Planner ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")
summarizes the corpus: 58,121 videos (2,943 h), about 28M captions and
489M tokens. Descriptions and instructions overlap heavily by design.
Their total span is about 6$`\times`$ the video duration, so every
moment is described several times at several scales. Each task partition
tiles its video exactly. 94.6% of task intents and 84.9% of instructions
are unique strings.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | Count | Per video (median) | Span (s) | Tokens / caption |
| Videos | 58,121 | – | 241.0 (duration) | – |
| Descriptions | 13,352,359 | 244 | 3.5 \[1.0, 8.0\] | 19.8 |
| Instructions | 13,155,310 | 237 | 3.5 \[1.0, 8.0\] | 15.2 |
| Task segments | 1,506,066 | 26 (5 partitions) | 31.5 \[12.0, 62.6\] | 16.1 |
````
