## Appendix B Implementation Details and Baseline Selection

### B.1 Minecraft

#### B.1.1 V2A Implementation Details

Architecture. Unless noted otherwise, the V2A model for Minecraft uses
an 80-million parameter V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-B model ([Assran et al.,
2025](#bib.bib1); [Mur-Labadia et al., 2026](#bib.bib41)) as a backbone.
The model takes up to 8 history frames and 16 future frames as input,
and predicts a chunk of up to 16 actions. The V2A predicts keyboard and
mouse actions from the MineRL 1.0 action space ([Guss et al.,
2019](#bib.bib17)). The button actions are parameterized as categorical
distributions, following the factorized button representation of VPT.
The $`x`$ and $`y`$ offsets for mouse movement are parameterized as a 2D
vector. For the diamond task, the final self-improving model is
retrained with the larger V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-L encoder
(Appendix [B.1.6](#A2.SS1.SSS6 "B.1.6 Diamond V2A Training ‣ B.1 Minecraft ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details and Baseline Selection ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")).

Exploration Noise. Exploration noise helps the agent learn novel
interactions with the environment. However, if the noise is too high
frequency, it may harm performance. Real-world actions are typically low
frequency—a player will often repeat the same action, such as moving
forward, over several time steps. We generate such low frequency
exploration noise with random walks. We inject Brownian motion with
standard deviation 1.0 for mouse exploration, and add noise
corresponding to random walks of button presses for discrete actions.

#### B.1.2 BASALT Evaluation

Our method and the BASALT baselines were evaluated using the 11 world
seeds from the BASALT 2022 challenge ([Milani et al.,
2022](#bib.bib38)). Specific task prompts and environment settings can
be found on the [MineRL
website](https://minerl.readthedocs.io/en/latest/environments/basalt.html).
The BASALT 2022 retrospective report ([Milani et al., 2022](#bib.bib38))
contains comprehensive details and code describing the winning solutions
to the challenge: GoUp, UniTeam, KAIROS, and others.

While the BASALT criteria are intentionally fuzzy, we evaluate each
method on objective criteria for fairness. For FindCave, success is
granted when the agent enters a cave or ravine. On MakeWaterfall, we
report success as when the player successfully places a water bucket,
and ends the episode facing the waterfall to “take a picture”. The
waterfall must be in view during the episode’s final frame for success
to be granted. Because Mirror does not rely on action labels and its
video planner makes the decisions, the planner also decides when an
episode ends: it predicts a gray screen where human players pressed Esc.
On MakeWaterfall, we therefore treat a gray screen predicted by the
video planner, or reaching the time limit, as the agent pressing Esc. As
the only exception, we ignore gray screens predicted before the agent
has given one second of movement input (about four blocks of walking),
to filter out false positives at the very start of an episode.

#### B.1.3 Diamond Challenge

The following subsections describe the diamond experiments of
Section [4.1.2](#S4.SS1.SSS2 "4.1.2 Self-improvement in Minecraft Survival Mode ‣ 4.1 Solving Long-Horizon Challenges in Minecraft ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models"):
the video planner’s data
(Appendix [B.1.4](#A2.SS1.SSS4 "B.1.4 Diamond Video Planner Data ‣ B.1 Minecraft ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details and Baseline Selection ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")),
the subgoal task planner
(Appendix [B.1.5](#A2.SS1.SSS5 "B.1.5 Subgoal Task Planner ‣ B.1 Minecraft ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details and Baseline Selection ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")),
the training of the self-improving V2A model
(Appendix [B.1.6](#A2.SS1.SSS6 "B.1.6 Diamond V2A Training ‣ B.1 Minecraft ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details and Baseline Selection ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")),
and the post-processing of the videos
(Appendix [B.1.7](#A2.SS1.SSS7 "B.1.7 GUI Video Post-Processing ‣ B.1 Minecraft ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details and Baseline Selection ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")).
Here we summarize what supervision enters the pipeline.

Neither the VP nor the self-improving V2A model is trained on expert
actions, rewards, or privileged game state; the only actions the
self-improving V2A model learns from are the ones the agent executed
itself. The VPT action and event logs come in at two places. First, as
the mouse cursor is missing inside menus in the VPT recordings, we draw
it using the logged mouse position, as VPT’s own data loader
does ([Baker et al., 2022](#bib.bib3)). This only restores what the
player saw on screen. Second, the logs help curate the VP’s data. They
direct the captioning VLM to salient moments
(Appendix [A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 Caption Generation ‣ Appendix A Video Planner ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models"))
and mark where each subgoal of the diamond task happens
(Appendix [B.1.4](#A2.SS1.SSS4 "B.1.4 Diamond Video Planner Data ‣ B.1 Minecraft ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details and Baseline Selection ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")).
This makes up for the limited capacity of our relatively small
captioning model, the roughly 8B-parameter VLM of Cosmos3-Nano ([NVIDIA,
2026](#bib.bib43)), which lacks Minecraft-specific domain knowledge. We
believe that stronger VLMs with broader domain knowledge will make these
log-based aids unnecessary. During rollouts, the subgoal task planner
reads the agent’s inventory, health, and whether a GUI is open. These
state inputs are used only to adjust the VP’s behavior by modulating its
text prompt and guidance scale.

#### B.1.4 Diamond Video Planner Data

Our VP was finetuned only on human gameplay from the VPT contractor
recordings ([Baker et al., 2022](#bib.bib3)). Starting from the video
planner pretrained on the VPT dataset
(Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Video Planner ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")),
we first finetune it for 30k steps on gameplay rendered with the
post-processing of
Appendix [B.1.7](#A2.SS1.SSS7 "B.1.7 GUI Video Post-Processing ‣ B.1 Minecraft ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details and Baseline Selection ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models"),
so that the planner gets used to the new cursor and hotbar. We then
post-train it for about 50k steps on a curated VPT subset split into
subgoals.

We split the task into 16 subgoals, from log to diamond
(Figure [11](#A2.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ B.1.5 Subgoal Task Planner ‣ B.1 Minecraft ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details and Baseline Selection ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")).
In the 2,212 hours of VPT data versions 6.10 to 10, an inventory gain in
the recorder log marks when a subgoal is completed, and a game statistic
tells whether the item was mined, crafted, placed, or taken from a
furnace. Each subgoal interval covers the activity leading up to the
gain, such as the last run of attacks before a mined block or the time
since the crafting screen opened. Training clips of 32 s lie at least
half inside an interval of their subgoal, and subgoals are sampled in
proportion to the fourth root of their footage, which roughly balances
them. The resulting clips span 665 hours, 403 of which fall inside
subgoal intervals. Footage is plentiful for gathering (153 hours for
cobblestone, 126 for log, and 68 for iron ore) but scarce for everything
else: 9.5 hours for diamond and 2.7–12.3 hours for each crafting,
placing, or smelting subgoal.

Each subgoal has a single caption of the form “Current subgoal: {item}.
{instruction}”, for example “Current subgoal: stone pickaxe. Craft a
stone pickaxe using cobblestone and sticks in the crafting grid.”
Captions carry no quantities, since the task planner decides when to
move on. Prediction windows inside a subgoal interval get its caption,
and some windows are left without text to train the unconditional branch
for classifier-free guidance.

#### B.1.5 Subgoal Task Planner

Figure 11: Subgoal task planner. (1) Once per plan, the planner reads
the agent’s inventory, health, and whether a GUI is open, and sends a
subgoal caption and a guidance scale $`w`$ to the video planner; the V2A
model never sees them. (2) Guidance-scale rules; the dashed one is used
only during training. (3) Subgoals in the order the planner picks them
from an empty inventory. Each 3$`\times`$3 craft happens at a crafting
table placed for it and picked up afterwards.

Dreamer V4 ([Hafner et al., 2025b](#bib.bib19)) also conditions its
agent on subgoals, prompting a one-hot task input through a fixed
sequence of 25 tasks during evaluation. As the code is not public, we
wrote our own heuristic subgoal planner
(Figure [11](#A2.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ B.1.5 Subgoal Task Planner ‣ B.1 Minecraft ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details and Baseline Selection ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")).
Once per plan, it picks the first unmet subgoal by chaining backward
from the diamond through the recipes, given the current inventory. It
collects spare wood before going underground and enough cobblestone for
both the stone pickaxe and the furnace, and it places a crafting table
before every 3$`\times`$3 craft and picks it up afterwards, since it
cannot tell whether an earlier table is still within reach. Its only
inputs are the inventory counts, the health, and whether a GUI is open.
Dreamer V4 does not say how it decides that a subgoal is done, but its
task set includes open_crafting_table and open_furnace, and its
evaluation prompts include use_stone_pickaxe and use_iron_pickaxe
(Tables 4 and 6 of [Hafner et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib19)). None of these
can be read from the inventory or a GUI flag. Our planner uses no such
game events and no learned classifier. The task planner’s only outputs
are the subgoal caption and the text CFG scale of the video planner. The
V2A model never sees either.

The text CFG scale is 7 by default. After the agent takes damage, it
drops to 0.01 until the lost health is repaid at 1 HP per 1.5 s, so the
video planner falls back on what players typically do when hurt, e.g.,
fight or flee. In a fraction of the training episodes, it also
oscillates between 7 and 1/7 on the subgoals where the agent stalls most
(cobblestone, iron ore, loading the furnace, iron ingot, and diamond).
Evaluation never uses this rule.

#### B.1.6 Diamond V2A Training

##### Online training.

The self-improving V2A model starts from a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-B
encoder ([Assran et al., 2025](#bib.bib1); [Mur-Labadia et al.,
2026](#bib.bib41)) with freshly initialized action heads and learns
online in 56 parallel environments. Training batches are sampled
uniformly from a replay buffer that keeps the latest four in-game
minutes of experience per environment. We keep the update-to-data ratio
at about 1, lower than in typical sample-efficient RL methods that
update many times per environment step. Our V2A objective has much lower
variance than RL objectives, so the model learns efficiently from each
transition, and compute is better spent on exploring new parts of the
task than on replaying old experience. The V2A model’s observations pass
through a Wan2.2 VAE round trip, so that they look like the generated
plans. Online training ran for 45k updates at batch 224, over 140
in-game hours.

##### Exploration.

Exploration comes from two sources. The first is behavioral: lowering
the text CFG scale pulls the plans toward the unconditional VP, which
reproduces the exploratory and recovery behavior of human players. The
second is action noise
(Appendix [B.1.1](#A2.SS1.SSS1 "B.1.1 V2A Implementation Details ‣ B.1 Minecraft ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details and Baseline Selection ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")),
whose main role is to keep a minimum probability on every action.
Actions with little or no visible effect, such as mouse clicks in an
empty space, easily collapse to a single mode. The V2A model trains on
its own executed actions and this results in a self-reinforcing
collapse. The action exploration noise keeps a minimal floor
probability, preventing any action from being starved. Note that both
kinds of exploration are double-edged: they diversify the data, but they
also slow the agent down and lower its chance of reaching deep subgoals.
We therefore explore mostly at the frontier, where the agent is believed
to be stuck. In the last four minutes before each milestone deadline,
the guidance scale oscillates between 7 and 0.05 on a log scale and the
action noise turns on and off, each with a random period of 0.5 to 3
minutes. In a fraction of the training episodes, the task planner also
oscillates the guidance scale on stall-prone subgoals
(Figure [11](#A2.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ B.1.5 Subgoal Task Planner ‣ B.1 Minecraft ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details and Baseline Selection ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")).
Action noise is applied only during these exploration periods and the
staggered entry below, and the V2A model trains on the noisy actions
that were actually executed, rather than the clean actions it predicted.
Even a small noise at this frontier is enough to prevent
self-reinforcing collapse. Finally, if all environments started their
episodes at once, the replay would be dominated by whichever subgoal
they were all working on. To balance the subgoals, we stagger the start
of training: environment $`g\in\{0,\dots,55\}`$ first plays an
unconditional world with action noise for $`(g+\tfrac{1}{2})\cdot 32`$ s
(16 s to 29.6 min) before its first task episode, which spreads the
environments across the task. This staggered entry is applied only once,
when training starts.

##### Episodes and savepoints.

To save compute, a training episode is split into segments that end at
four milestones read from the inventory (a crafting table, a wooden
pickaxe, a stone pickaxe, and three iron ore) and a final segment that
ends at the diamond. The segments have limits of 10, 10, 10, 15, and 15
minutes plus the four-minute exploration period; a missed deadline or a
third death ends the episode. We also save the world when an episode
reaches the stone pickaxe, keep the 14 latest save points, and start a
new episode from a random save with probability 0.25 times the filled
fraction of this pool. These rules are not used at evaluation. We note
that these rules could tilt the training distribution through selection
bias. The limits, however, are loose. During training, each limit was
1.9 to 2.8 times the mean time the agent took to reach the milestone,
and at least 92% of the reached milestones came within the limit. The
deadlines thus rarely cut episodes that were still making progress and
are unlikely to accelerate learning the way a reward would. If anything,
the tilt works against speed, as an episode nearing its deadline enters
the exploration period, which slows the agent down. Even if such a
positive tilt exists, the four milestones are far coarser than the 15 to
20 rewarded subgoals of RL agents ([Baker et al., 2022](#bib.bib3);
[Hafner et al., 2025b](#bib.bib19)). For the oracle VP, we do not use
the milestone deadlines and keep only a global episode limit of up to 10
minutes. The oracle is an RL policy that progresses much faster than
human players, so deadlines set for our VP, which follows the pace of
human gameplay, are rarely reached.

##### Final model.

After online training, we retrain a fresh V2A model with the larger
V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-L encoder ([Assran et al., 2025](#bib.bib1); [Mur-Labadia
et al., 2026](#bib.bib41)) on the last 110 of the 140 in-game hours of
online experience, excluding the first 30 hours, which are dominated by
exploration. It trains on the agent’s own executed actions for 20k steps
at batch 128 and is the self-improving model in
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Self-improvement with a generative VP. ‣ 4.1.2 Self-improvement in Minecraft Survival Mode ‣ 4.1 Solving Long-Horizon Challenges in Minecraft ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models").

#### B.1.7 GUI Video Post-Processing

![Refer to caption](2610.24177v1/gui_postprocess_pipeline.png)

Figure 12: Video post-processing for the diamond task. (a) The original
VPT video recordings do not include the cursor inside GUI menus. (b) As
in VPT’s data loader ([Baker et al., 2022](#bib.bib3)), we draw the
cursor from the mouse position log. However, VPT’s original
16$`\times`$16 cursor is too small for the Wan2.2 VAE, which blurs or
drops it
(Figure [13](#A2.F13 "Figure 13 ‣ B.1.7 GUI Video Post-Processing ‣ B.1 Minecraft ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details and Baseline Selection ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models")).
Thus, for the diamond task we draw a high-visibility cursor: VPT’s
cursor enlarged 2$`\times`$, tinted coral, and outlined in black and
white. (c) The VAE also blurs the small item counts or turns them into
other digits, so we crop the 184$`\times`$24-pixel hotbar from the
video, enlarge it 3$`\times`$ with nearest-neighbor upsampling, and
paste it back at the bottom center, moving the health and food bars up.
(d) Finally, we resize the $`640\times 360`$ frames to $`320\times 192`$
with bilinear interpolation and antialiasing. Of the filters we tried,
it is the blurriest but keeps all task-relevant detail and causes the
fewest VAE artifacts (reconstruction PSNR 32.7 dB, versus 24.5–30.4 dB
for bilinear without antialiasing, bicubic, area, and Lanczos).

![Refer to caption](2610.24177v1/vae_cursor_missing.png)

Figure 13: The Wan2.2 VAE loses the VPT cursor. The same frame with
(a) VPT’s cursor and (b) the high-visibility cursor, before and after a
round trip through the Wan2.2 VAE. VPT’s small cursor nearly vanishes in
the reconstruction, which is why we draw a larger, outlined cursor for
GUI-heavy tasks.

These steps change only the video, not the game. As with the VPT
recordings, the environment renders frames without a cursor and we draw
ours on top, and we apply the same post-processing to the VP’s training
data and to the agent’s observations during training and evaluation. The
steps are needed because of the Wan2.2 VAE ([Wan Team,
2025](#bib.bib61)), whose latent space Cosmos3 is trained in. The VAE
does not preserve small, high-precision details such as text and the
cursor, which matter for computer-use tasks. With the oracle VP, which
does not go through the VAE, the agent learns to mine diamonds without
any of this post-processing. We therefore see the post-processing as a
limitation of the Wan2.2 VAE rather than of our method, and we expect it
to become unnecessary once video VAEs are trained on computer-use data.

### B.2 Robotics and Atari

#### B.2.1 Environments and Evaluation

We evaluate on 13 DeepMind Control (DMC) tasks, four single-task OGBench
environments, and seven Atari games. Each online method receives
$`10^{6}`$ environment actions and is evaluated every 25,000 actions
over 20 episodes, with five training seeds per task. Random-V2A collects
its interaction budget before offline fitting on different-sized
subsets. We average tasks equally, reporting native return on DMC,
success rate on OGBench, and
$`100R_{\mathrm{agent}}/R_{\mathrm{expert}}`$ on Atari.

##### OGBench.

We use four visual single-task environments: cube-single and cube-double
require rearranging one and two cubes; scene requires manipulating a
drawer, window, and locking buttons; and antmaze-large requires
navigating a quadruped robot to a goal. Observations are $`64\times 64`$
RGB images. We use task 2 for Cube Single, Cube Double, and Scene, and
task 1 for AntMaze Large.

##### DeepMind Control.

Following [Giammarino et al. (2024)](#bib.bib16), we use 13 tasks from
DMC ([Tassa et al., 2018](#bib.bib54)): Ball-in-Cup Catch, Finger Spin,
Cartpole Balance and Swingup, Pendulum Swingup, Walker Stand/Walk/Run,
Hopper Stand/Hop, Quadruped Walk/Run, and Cheetah Run. Agents receive
$`84\times 84`$ RGB observations with three-frame histories.

##### Atari.

Following [Escontrela et al. (2023)](#bib.bib12), we evaluate on
Assault, Atlantis, Boxing, Freeway, Kangaroo, Pong, and Zaxxon from the
Arcade Learning Environment ([Bellemare et al., 2013](#bib.bib4)). We
use $`84\times 84`$ grayscale observations, four-frame histories, the
minimal action set, sticky-action probability 0.25, and action repeat
four. One million Atari decisions correspond to approximately four
million emulator frames.

#### B.2.2 Shared Implementation

##### Action models.

Mirror, BCO, Grounding, and Random-V2A use flow-based action models with
method-specific conditioning. Continuous-control models use an
IMPALA-style visual encoder and four 1024-unit flow layers. Atari uses a
smaller encoder, one 512-unit flow layer, and factorized one-hot action
codes projected to legal actions. Training uses Adam with learning rate
$`3\times 10^{-4}`$, batch size 256, gradient clipping at 10, and
random-shift augmentation. Action sampling uses ten Euler integration
steps, from zero initialization at evaluation. LAIfO uses its separate
single-action learner.

The action horizon $`K`$ is five on OGBench; three on DMC except
Cartpole Balance (seven), Cartpole Swingup (ten), and Pendulum Swingup
(twenty); and two on Atari except Atlantis and Kangaroo (four).

##### Expert information.

Experts are BRO ([Nauman et al., 2024](#bib.bib42)) on DMC, FQL ([Park
et al., 2025b](#bib.bib47)) on OGBench, and DQN ([Mnih et al.,
2013](#bib.bib40)) on Atari. BCO and LAIfO receive observation-only
demonstrations: 50 episodes per Atari game and 1,000/500/500/50 episodes
for Cube Single/Cube Double/Scene/AntMaze Large. On OGBench, LAIfO uses
full-horizon trajectories that continue after success, whereas BCO uses
the original shorter demonstrations. DMC uses 50 episodes for BCO and
100 for LAIfO. No method uses expert action labels, task rewards, or
proprioceptive state.

##### Learned video planners.

Mirror and Grounding use task-specific latent flow predictors with four
residual blocks of width 512. A spatial autoencoder with encoder widths
$`64,128,128,128`$ maps frames at their native resolution to
$`4\times 4\times 2`$ latents on OGBench and DMC and
$`7\times 7\times 2`$ latents on Atari. The predictor models normalized
latent differences from the current frame. Autoencoders train for
250,000 updates and predictors for $`10^{7}`$ updates; flow training
uses Adam with peak learning rate $`3\times 10^{-4}`$, cosine decay,
batch size 256, gradient clipping at 1, and exponential-moving-average
weights with decay 0.999, and we keep the checkpoints with the lowest
validation loss. Prediction uses ten Euler steps and averages eight
latent samples per predicted frame. Autoencoders are frozen during flow
training, and both models remain frozen during downstream learning. Each
task shares one planner checkpoint across downstream seeds. Atari
planners use three context frames, while action models use four.

#### B.2.3 Methods and Hyperparameter Selection

##### Mirror.

After 5,000 random actions, Mirror repeatedly obtains $`K`$ future
frames, predicts a $`K`$-action sequence from the current visual history
and these frames, and executes it before replanning. Achieved
observations and executed actions enter a 100,000-transition replay
buffer, with 0.2 V2A model updates per environment action. Training
actions are sampled stochastically from the flow policy on all
benchmarks. On OGBench and DMC, each step also adds Gaussian noise to
one randomly chosen action coordinate ($`\sigma=0.1`$ on OGBench,
task-specific on DMC). Atari relies on the stochastic flow sampling
alone. Evaluation uses deterministic V2A model readout without
collection noise.

For learned-planner experiments, we build the planner’s training set by
iterative dataset aggregation: starting from 200,000 expert transitions,
each round executes the current planner–V2A controller and branches
20-step expert recoveries (30 steps in later rounds for three DMC tasks)
from its states with probability 0.1 per step, with later rounds adding
action noise and finally a mix of action corruptions (Gaussian noise,
random, scaled, sticky, or delayed actions) to the executed controller
actions. The final planner is trained from scratch on the aggregated
corpus (3.5–13 million transitions per task, 5% held out for
validation). It conditions on three frames and predicts one future frame
at a time, generating $`K`$-frame plans autoregressively.

##### Behavioral Cloning from Observation.

BCO ([Torabi et al., 2018](#bib.bib58)) alternates learner interaction,
V2A model fitting, and policy fitting. The V2A model infers action
sequences from expert observations, and an observation-conditioned
policy learns these pseudo-labels and executes action chunks open loop.
Both networks retain their parameters and optimizer state across rounds.
Episode-level validation selects each fit, and pending fits finish
before final evaluation.

We tune the initial collection size $`i_{\mathrm{pre}}`$ and collection
ratio $`\alpha`$, giving approximately $`\alpha i_{\mathrm{pre}}`$
actions between refits. Nine pairs are evaluated with three seeds on
Cube Single, Finger Spin, and Pong, ranked by the final three
evaluations. Selected $`(i_{\mathrm{pre}},\alpha)`$ values are
$`(40{,}000,0.1)`$ for OGBench, $`(20{,}000,0.2)`$ for DMC, and
$`(20{,}000,0.4)`$ for Atari.

##### LAIfO.

LAIfO ([Giammarino et al., 2024](#bib.bib16)) learns an imitation reward
by discriminating expert and learner observation transitions, then
trains a single-action off-policy learner. Transition distance $`n`$
controls discriminator inputs and critic bootstrapping. DMC uses
released task-specific settings with our BRO experts; Atari uses a
dueling Double-DQN ([Wang et al., 2016](#bib.bib65); [van Hasselt
et al., 2015](#bib.bib60)) adaptation with greedy evaluation.

We tune exploration decay, transition distance, batch size, and a paired
learning-rate/feature-dimension setting on Cube Single and Pong using
24- and 36-configuration grids, respectively, with three seeds per
configuration. Selection uses performance at one million actions. Both
suites select a 100k exploration decay, batch size 512, learning rate
$`8\times 10^{-5}`$, and feature dimension 100. Transition distance is
three for OGBench and one for Atari; discriminator learning rate is
$`4\times 10^{-4}`$.

##### Grounding.

Grounding ([Luo & Du, 2024](#bib.bib36)) trains a goal-conditioned
action model from random and plan-guided rollouts. Each training segment
uses its final achieved image as the goal and executed actions as
targets. Following an initial random-only fitting phase, replay sampling
uses 30% random and 70% guided data. On OGBench, we follow the released
LIBERO implementation, conditioning the model on a single current frame,
with each guided collection following a single video plan without
replanning. During evaluation, we periodically replan from the latest
observation, with the number of plans set by each environment’s time
limit. For DMC and Atari, we use three and four frame observation
histories, respectively. To accommodate their longer task horizon, we
replan during both collection and evaluation after every two subgoals in
oracle planner experiments and after every subgoal in generative planner
experiments.

We tune random-action hold duration and optimizer-update intervals
between guided and random collection using 27-configuration, three-seed
sweeps on Cube Single, Finger Spin, and Pong, ranked by the final five
evaluations. Selected
$`(\text{hold},\text{guided interval},\text{random interval})`$ values
are $`(5,100,500)`$, $`(10,100,500)`$, and $`(5,200,1000)`$ for OGBench,
DMC, and Atari, respectively. OGBench collection intervals scale with
task length.

Grounding’s learned planners use the shared architecture and training
recipe with task-specific subgoal targets. DMC and Atari reuse the
aggregated expert/recovery corpus, conditioning on three frames to
predict an expert-continuation subgoal $`K`$ actions ahead. OGBench uses
1,000 expert episodes per task with a 950/50 training/validation split,
conditions on one frame, and jointly predicts 7/14/20/70 subgoals for
Cube Single/Cube Double/Scene/AntMaze Large. Following the original
implementation, targets are spaced evenly from a sampled starting frame
to shortly after expert success, with the final frame used for
unsuccessful episodes.

##### Random-V2A.

This baseline fits the same V2A model as Mirror independently on
cumulative subsets of 100k to 1M transitions from a frozen uniformly
random corpus. We hold out 5% of episodes and select checkpoints by
validation flow loss. Evaluation translates visual plans into action
chunks using deterministic V2A readout; generative-VP results
re-evaluate the same fitted models with the learned planner in place of
the oracle.

##### VIPER.

VIPER ([Escontrela et al., 2023](#bib.bib12)) learns a generative video
model from expert observations and uses observation likelihoods as an RL
reward. We include it as an Atari-only likelihood-reward reference,
using estimates from its published results.

#### C.1.4 Text-Conditioned Minecraft Evaluation

We evaluate text control in two worlds: Woodland and Camp. The worlds
are designed to contain various locations of interest, such as trees, a
pool, a hill, and a cave. In each world, the player starts with an iron
sword, iron tools, torches, wood planks, bread, and a water bucket. We
evaluate 10 episodes per text prompt. In each episode, we first make the
player pan the camera left and right to observe their environment. Then
it must complete each task given by the text prompt within 30 seconds.
The video planner uses a classifier-free guidance scale of 7.0. We
include more results on text-conditioned task guidance in
Figure [14](#A3.F14 "Figure 14 ‣ C.1.4 Text-Conditioned Minecraft Evaluation ‣ C.1 Minecraft ‣ Appendix C Additional Results ‣ Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models").

![Refer to caption](2610.24177v1/camp_results.png)

Figure 14: Text-conditioned planning on Camp. We demonstrate
text-conditioned planning on the camp environment. While our
self-improving approach is able to solve many tasks, it struggles on
tasks with fine-grained environment interactions such as placing torches
in the cave. Meanwhile, VIPER, our action-free baseline, struggles to
learn the action space of Minecraft. BC solves some tasks, but remains
limited in its generalization ability.
